hints: Focus on what controls equilibrium yield, not rate. Think about how Le Chatelier's principle responds to temperature and pressure changes.
Notice the enthalpy change is very negative, so the forward reaction gives out heat. That tells you which way low temperature will push the equilibrium.
Now count the total moles of gas on each side, 9 on the left versus 10 on the right, and ask which pressure pushes equilibrium toward more NO.
walkthrough:
**Decide the temperature effect from delta H**

Think of heat as a product because the forward reaction is exothermic. Lowering temperature removes heat, so equilibrium shifts forward to replace it.

$$4\text{NH}_3(g) + 5\text{O}_2(g) \rightleftharpoons 4\text{NO}(g) + 6\text{H}_2\text{O}(g) \quad \Delta H = -1636 \text{ kJ mol}^{-1}$$

**Decide the pressure effect from moles of gas**

Count gas moles. Left side has $4 + 5 = 9$ mol, right side has $4 + 6 = 10$ mol. Lowering pressure always favours the side with more gas moles.

$$\text{left: 9 mol gas} \rightleftharpoons \text{right: 10 mol gas}$$

**Combine both for maximum yield**

Low temperature favours the exothermic forward reaction, and low pressure favours the side with 10 moles. Together they give the greatest equilibrium amount of $\text{NO}$.

options.A: High temperature shifts the exothermic equilibrium backward toward reactants, and high pressure shifts it toward fewer moles (left). Both changes lower NO yield.
options.B: Low pressure is correct for more gas moles on the right, but high temperature is wrong. High temperature favours the endothermic backward reaction, so NO yield falls.
options.C: Low temperature is correct for an exothermic forward reaction, but high pressure is wrong. High pressure favours the left side with only 9 moles, so NO yield falls.
options.D: Low temperature favours the exothermic forward reaction and low pressure favours the side with more gas moles (10 mol on the right). Both shift equilibrium forward, giving the greatest yield of NO.
